title: BIBLICAL SUBMISSION: What Christians Actually Owe Their Leaders—and What They Never Owe Them
paragraphs: BIBLICAL SUBMISSION: What Christians Actually Owe Their Leaders—and What They Never Owe Them

You were told, “Touch not God’s anointed.” You were told questioning a leader meant questioning God. You may even have been taught that submission means silence. But when Scripture itself is allowed to speak, something far more beautiful—and far more demanding—emerges: biblical submission is real, Christian leadership is real, obedience matters, and yet Jesus Christ alone remains Lord.
There is a sentence that has kept wounded Christians awake at night.
“Maybe I’m the rebellious one.”
Sometimes it comes after a pastor has been questioned.
Sometimes after a church member says no.
Sometimes after someone notices that what is happening behind the pulpit does not resemble the Jesus being preached from it.
And sometimes it comes after years of being taught that a faithful Christian never challenges spiritual authority.
So you sit there with the Bible open and your heart pounding.
You love Jesus.
You do not want to rebel against God.
You do not want bitterness growing inside you.
You do not want to dishonor someone whom God has called to shepherd His people.
But something is wrong.
And now the question becomes terrifying:
What does God actually require me to give my spiritual leaders?
The answer matters because there are two cliffs on either side of this road.

On one side is rebellion disguised as discernment—the arrogant spirit that refuses correction, despises authority, church-hops whenever confronted, and calls every uncomfortable truth “spiritual abuse.”

On the other side is unquestioning allegiance disguised as submission—the belief that a pastor, elder, ministry leader, husband, parent, politician, or Christian celebrity can demand what belongs only to Christ.
Scripture permits neither.
And somewhere between those cliffs stands Jesus.
Not weak.
Not confused.
Not intimidated by authority.
Not contemptuous of legitimate authority.
Jesus—the King who washed feet.
The Lord who submitted Himself to the Father.
The Shepherd who laid His life down for sheep instead of using sheep to build His kingdom.
That changes everything.
Hebrews 13:17 is one of the passages Christians most often encounter in conversations about spiritual authority. The Greek contains two especially important words:
πείθεσθε — peithesthe
and
ὑπείκετε — hypeikete

The verse calls believers to respond appropriately to their leaders and yield to them because those leaders “keep watch” over souls and will themselves have to give an account. The Mounce interlinear renders the first term in the sense of continuing to obey and the second as submitting or yielding. The verse therefore gives genuine weight to spiritual leadership; it is not permission to treat pastors and elders as irrelevant.
But notice what is sitting inside the very verse sometimes used to demand unquestioning loyalty.
Accountability.
Leaders watch over souls “as those who must give an account.”
That sentence should make every Christian leader tremble before it makes any congregation member tremble.
The sheep belong to God.
The church belongs to Christ.
The pulpit belongs to Christ.
The ministry belongs to Christ.
The reputation belongs to Christ.
The money belongs to Christ.
The wounded person sitting in the back row belongs to Christ.
The pastor does not own the flock.
He will answer for how he treated it.
That is why biblical submission can never mean surrendering your conscience to another human being.
There is only one throne at the center of Christianity.
And your pastor is not sitting on it.
Neither am I.
Neither are you.
Jesus is.
This is where some people become uncomfortable, because abuses of authority have made the word submission itself sound dangerous.
But throwing away biblical submission because somebody corrupted it would be another tragedy.
Scripture really does teach submission.
Ephesians 5:21 uses the Greek:
ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ
“being subject to one another out of reverence for Christ.”

The key word ὑποτάσσω — hypotassō carries the idea of being subject or placing oneself in an ordered relationship. Yet notice the atmosphere surrounding Christian submission: it is rooted in reverence for Christ.
Christ remains the gravitational center.
Biblical submission is not personality worship.
It is not intellectual suicide.
It is not pretending sin is holiness because the sinner owns a microphone.
It is not protecting a ministry brand while victims bleed quietly.
It is not allowing someone to manipulate you with “God told me” when what follows contradicts what God has already said.
And it certainly is not giving another human being the obedience that belongs uniquely to Jesus Christ.
The apostles themselves demonstrated the boundary.
When the authorities commanded them to stop proclaiming Christ, Peter and the apostles answered with one of the clearest principles in the New Testament:
“We must obey God rather than men.” — Acts 5:29
There it is.
Not rebellion for rebellion’s sake.
Not disrespect.
Not anarchy.
A hierarchy of allegiance.
When human authority and divine authority collide, God wins.
Every time.
And this becomes even clearer when Scripture turns from the responsibilities of the flock to the responsibilities of the shepherd.
Peter does not tell elders, “Make sure everybody knows who is in charge.”
He tells them to shepherd God’s flock willingly and eagerly, then explicitly warns them against domineering over those entrusted to their care. Instead, leaders are to become examples to the flock.
Read that again slowly.
Not domineering.
Examples.
The New Testament model of leadership is therefore not:
“Look how many people obey me.”
It is:
“Look how faithfully I imitate Christ.”
Jesus Himself destroyed the worldly definition of greatness.
The rulers of the nations “lord it over” people.
Christ tells His disciples that it must not be that way among them.
The greatest becomes a servant.
Then Jesus does something almost unbearable in its beauty.
The One who could command angels kneels.
God the Son takes a towel.
The hands through whom creation came wash dirty feet.
And suddenly Christian authority has a permanent shape.
A cross.
This is the scandal.
The highest King became the lowest servant.
The Lord did not need to crush people to prove He was Lord.
He loved.
He served.
He corrected.
He confronted.
He commanded.
He forgave.
And finally He stretched out His hands and allowed sinners to nail Him to wood.

So when someone uses “submission” to justify domination, coercion, concealment, exploitation, sexual misconduct, financial manipulation, retaliation against legitimate questions, or unquestioning loyalty to a personality, the problem is not that Christianity takes authority too seriously.
The problem is that such leadership does not take Christ’s authority seriously enough.
Maybe this is where your story enters.
Maybe somebody wounded you in church.
And perhaps what makes the wound so confusing is that they used Scripture while doing it.
Maybe you asked a sincere question and were labeled rebellious.
Maybe you reported something troubling and suddenly became “divisive.”
Maybe you watched everyone protect the influential person while the wounded person disappeared.
Maybe you left.
And perhaps you have carried shame ever since.
But there is another possibility we must have enough humility to confront.
Maybe nobody abused you.
Maybe you simply hated being corrected.
Maybe a faithful pastor told you something your flesh did not want to hear.

Maybe Scripture exposed your relationship, your pride, your sexual sin, your greed, your bitterness, your unforgiveness, your gossip, or your compromise—and instead of repenting, you renamed conviction “control.”
That happens too.
We must tell the whole truth.
Not every confrontation is abuse.
Not every boundary is manipulation.
Not every pastor who disagrees with you is controlling.
Not every uncomfortable sermon is toxic.
Sometimes the shepherd is warning you because the cliff is real.
Sometimes you are not being persecuted.
Sometimes you are being corrected.
And sometimes the most loving thing a Christian leader can say is:
No. This is sin. Come back.
Biblical discernment cuts both directions.
It protects sheep from wolves.
And it protects sheep from becoming stubborn enough to wander away from the Shepherd.
That is why the mature Christian does not begin with, “Do I like what my leader said?”
The mature Christian asks:
“Is it faithful to Christ and His Word?”
That question changes everything.
If your pastor faithfully teaches Scripture, pray for him.
Encourage him.
Receive correction humbly.
Make his work a joy rather than manufacturing unnecessary conflict.
Refuse gossip.
Refuse the consumer mentality that treats churches like restaurants and pastors like customer-service representatives.
Honor faithful elders.

Give thanks for shepherds who study while everyone else sleeps, answer calls when families are collapsing, visit hospitals, bury loved ones, counsel marriages, preach when exhausted, carry secrets they cannot repeat, and quietly wonder whether they are making any difference.
Hebrews 13:17 says leaders are watching over souls knowing that they must answer for that stewardship. That is a staggering burden.
Pray for them.
But do not worship them.
Listen to them.
But keep your Bible open.
Honor them.
But never hand them Christ’s throne.
Receive biblical correction.
But test teaching by Scripture.
Follow godly examples.
But remember whose footsteps ultimately matter.
Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply freeing about this.
Healthy biblical submission does not require you to become less devoted to Jesus.
It makes you more devoted to Jesus.
Healthy leadership does not fear Scripture being opened.
It welcomes it.
Healthy shepherds are not terrified when sheep know the Shepherd’s voice.
They desperately want them to.
Because faithful pastors understand something celebrity Christianity can make us forget:
The goal of Christian leadership is not to make people dependent upon the leader.
The goal is to help people mature in Christ.
Paul could say, in effect, imitate me as I imitate Christ.
That qualification matters.
Christ is the standard.
Christ is the destination.
Christ is the Head of the Church.
Christ purchased His people with blood.
And when a human leader forgets that, the Gospel brings him back to reality.
Pastors need grace too.
Leaders sin too.
Leaders need repentance too.
Leaders need accountability too.
Leaders need brothers who can look them in the eyes and say, “No.”
A leader who cannot be corrected is not demonstrating strength.
He is standing somewhere spiritually dangerous.
Peter—the apostle who wrote about shepherding—knew what correction felt like.
He had failed spectacularly.
He had denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the scandal.
A leading apostle publicly collapsing at the exact moment courage was required.
If Christianity were merely a public-relations campaign, Peter's story would have been buried.
Instead, Scripture preserved it.
Why?
Because Christianity is not the story of impressive people protecting impressive reputations.
It is the story of sinners being redeemed by an impressive Savior.
Peter failed.
Peter wept.
Peter was restored.
And Jesus still used him.
That is grace.
Perhaps that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to hear.
Maybe you were a leader who failed.
Maybe pride entered your ministry slowly.
Maybe applause became addictive.
Maybe criticism started feeling like betrayal.
Maybe somewhere along the road, “Jesus’ ministry” quietly became “my ministry.”
Repent.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
The cross is not only for the people sitting in your congregation.
It is for you.
There is forgiveness for pastors.
There is restoration where biblical restoration is appropriate.
There is mercy for elders.
There is cleansing for leaders who stop defending darkness and drag it into the light.
Jesus is still rewriting stories.
And perhaps you are not the leader.
Perhaps you are the wounded sheep.
Then hear this carefully:
Do not allow what a human shepherd did to convince you that the Good Shepherd is like him.
Jesus is not the pastor who betrayed you.
Jesus is not the ministry that manipulated you.
Jesus is not the Christian who exploited your trust.
Jesus is not the person who covered darkness while quoting Bible verses.
Look at Christ Himself.
The Shepherd in John 10 does not devour the sheep.
He lays down His life for them.
That is your Jesus.
And maybe your next act of faith is not pretending nothing happened.
Maybe it is bringing what happened into truth.
Seeking wise, biblically grounded counsel.
Reporting criminal conduct to the appropriate civil authorities when necessary.
Rejecting vengeance while refusing concealment.
Forgiving without calling evil good.
Remembering that forgiveness and restored trust are not identical things.
And refusing to let another person's sin become the graveyard of your faith.
Because Satan would love a double victory.
First, let someone wound you in the name of Christianity.
Then convince you to abandon Christ because of what that person did.
Do not give darkness the second victory.
Run past the failed representative.
Run to Jesus.
And if you are the Christian who has spent years refusing every authority because someone once abused authority, Christ can heal that too.
You do not have to live permanently suspicious.
You can learn discernment without becoming cynical.
You can honor without idolizing.
You can submit without surrendering your conscience.
You can ask questions without becoming rebellious.
You can receive correction without becoming controlled.
You can forgive without pretending.
You can love the Church while acknowledging where churches have failed.
You can believe in biblical leadership without building idols out of leaders.
This is the narrow road.
And Jesus walks it with us.
So what do Christians actually owe their leaders?

Biblically, we owe faithful leaders honor, prayer, appropriate cooperation and submission, teachability, love, encouragement, and a willingness to receive leadership consistent with Christ and His Word.
What do we never owe them?
Worship.
Blind allegiance.
The surrender of conscience.
Participation in sin.
Silence about criminal wrongdoing.
Permission to contradict Scripture.
Or the obedience that belongs to God alone.
There is one Chief Shepherd.

First Peter 5 ultimately points earthly shepherds beyond themselves to the Chief Shepherd who will appear. Earthly leaders are under-shepherds. Their authority is borrowed, accountable, temporary, and answerable to Him.
Jesus owns the Church.
That truth protects both pastors and congregations.
It protects pastors from the unbearable delusion that everything depends on them.
And it protects congregations from the equally dangerous delusion that their pastor is their mediator before God.
There is already a Mediator.
His name is Jesus.
There is already a spotless High Priest.
Jesus.
There is already a King.
Jesus.
There is already a Savior.
Jesus.
And He did not save you by demanding that you climb high enough to reach Him.
He came down for you.
That is the Gospel.
You sinned against a holy God.
So did I.
Our deepest problem is not bad leadership, bad churches, bad institutions, or bad experiences—terrible as those things can be.
Our deepest problem is sin.
And Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, took the judgment sinners deserved upon Himself at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
Grace walked out of a tomb.
And now the invitation is not, “Find a perfect pastor.”
You never will.
The invitation is:
Come to the perfect Savior.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Jesus.
And then learn, inside His redeemed community, how imperfect Christians can honor imperfect leaders who are themselves bowing before the perfect King.
That is biblical submission.
Not slavery to men.
Freedom under Christ.
Not silence in darkness.
Walking in light.
Not leader worship.
Christ worship.
Not rebellion masquerading as independence.
Humility anchored in truth.
And maybe this article found you because you have been wrestling with this for years.
If it exposed rebellion in you, do not defend it.
Repent.
If it exposed unhealthy allegiance to a human personality, do not hide from that either.
Return your worship to Jesus.
If it reopened a church wound, bring that wound to the Good Shepherd instead of allowing it to rot beneath Christian language.
And if your heart is exhausted and all you can manage today is honesty, then be honest.
Your honesty may become permission for another wounded believer to stop hiding.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith in Christ.
But if you sincerely want to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, one practical response is to help sound biblical truth travel farther.

Your support helps us keep producing and distributing Christ-centered biblical content and expanding resources intended to point people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus Christ. But Christians can glorify God through willing generosity and by helping faithful Gospel work reach people who need it.
Your leader may help shepherd your soul—but only Jesus purchased it with His blood.
So honor faithful leaders.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Receive biblical correction.
Refuse arrogant rebellion.
Expose darkness rather than protecting it.
Forgive.
Discern.
Keep your Bible open.
Keep your knees bent.
Keep your eyes on Christ.

Because when every platform disappears, every title is surrendered, every congregation is scattered, every ministry brand is forgotten, and every human shepherd stands before the One to whom he must give an account, there will still be only one name above every name.
Jesus.
And perhaps the most dangerous spiritual mistake is not merely refusing to submit to a leader.
Perhaps it is submitting to anyone so completely that you forget who died for you.
Human shepherds may carry the staff for a season. The nail-scarred Shepherd carries you into eternity.
